En 1995, Nourmohamed Ibragimov arrive au: In 1995, Nourmohamed Ibragimov arrived in Canada with his wife and three boys. They became the first Uyghur family to settle in the country. Nourmohamed, who was 45 at the time, had already lived several lives. Born in 1950 in East Turkestan, a region also known as Xinjiang, he was only 5 years old when his family fled Chinese repression and left their homeland for the USSR.
« La Chine avait commencé la destruction: “China had begun the destruction and the genocide. So my parents decided to leave the country,” he says. Even though he did not live there for long, Nourmohamed remains deeply attached to his country of origin, East Turkestan. He describes it as a vast territory rich in natural resources, with a unique culture.
C’est avec une pointe de tristesse que l: With a hint of sadness, he tells us about his childhood in the part of the Soviet Union now called Kazakhstan. “I grew up in Kazakhstan, where I studied. After university, I started working in the legal system; my career there lasted many years,” he explains.
Sur place, l’avocat de formation vit la: There, the lawyer by training experienced the repression of the Soviet regime. Before turning to law, Nourmohamed had wanted to become a soldier. The discrimination rampant in the USSR had dissuaded him. Tired of being mistreated, he turned to Canada. “Canada is a very democratic country. It’s a very big country, a country of immigrants. Those are the reasons I decided to leave Kazakhstan and settle here,” he says.
En arrivant au Québec, il relève le défi: Upon arriving in Quebec, he took on the challenge of learning French, a language added to his polyglot repertoire, which includes Uyghur, Kazakh, German and Russian. Keen to take part in community life, he began volunteering. But finding a job was hard. His law degree was not recognized, and Nourmohamed started working as a security guard in the Montréal area. He has built a career in that field for more than 25 years.
Malgré tout, il regarde toujours les cho: Despite everything, he always looks on the bright side. “When we arrived, we were the only Uyghur family.
Maintenant, nous sommes environ 200 fami: Now, there are about 200 families of us,” he says proudly. His three sons have done well for themselves, and at 71, he is now a grandfather. “I am so proud of my children. I often pray to Allah to thank Him for giving them to me,” says the fulfilled father.
<strong>Transmettre « l’histoire de notr: Passing on “the history of our country, the history of our language”
Particulièrement près de sa culture, Nou: Particularly close to his culture, Nourmohamed wanted to pass it on to his sons. When they were young, Nourmohamed set aside weekends for cultural activities as a family. “I told them the history of our country, the history of our language. I introduced them to a few cultural elements like singing, music, photography,” he recalls.
Il passait les fins de semaine à leur ap: He spent weekends teaching them to cook laghman, a very colourful traditional noodle dish, and to perform the traditional songs played at major events.
Cette tradition de transmission culturel: This tradition of cultural transmission comes from his own parents, who, during his childhood in Kazakhstan, made sure to pass on the Uyghur language and culture to him.
« Lorsque nous avons déménagé au Kazakhs: “When we moved to Kazakhstan, there were already a million Uyghurs. There, we had our own society, our own theatre, our newspapers, our radio. Thanks to that, I kept my mother tongue,” he explains. The situation is very different in his adopted country.
« Ici, c’est plus difficile de préserver: “Here, it’s harder to preserve our culture because there are so few of us,” says the septuagenarian. Despite his efforts, the language was hard to pass down, for lack of people to speak it with. “My children understand, but they speak slowly, with difficulty,” he says with a hint of regret.
Aujourd’hui, à 71 ans, son rêve le plus: Today, at 71, his dearest dream is to found a Uyghur cultural centre in Montréal. “I want to start a school for children. So that they don’t forget our mother tongue. It’s difficult, because of the high rents downtown.
J’espère donc qu’on pourra bientôt achet: So I hope we can soon buy a building to set up a Uyghur cultural centre,” he confides, hoping to pass his culture on to a new generation of Uyghurs.
